transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

I'm here because I'm really struggling with how my face looks. I have these horrible scars and acne, and my nose looks completely deformed to me, even though everyone else tells me it looks totally normal. It's just taking over my life and I can't stop focusing on it.

When you get stuck thinking about your face, do you find yourself doing things like checking mirrors a lot, comparing your appearance to other people, picking at your skin, or seeking reassurance? If so, about how much time do these thoughts and behaviors take each day?

Yes, I do all of those things, and it easily takes up several hours of my day. I'm constantly checking the mirror, picking at my skin to try and 'fix' it, and comparing my face to everyone I see. I also repeatedly ask my family and friends for reassurance because I'm just so anxious about how I look.

Over the past 2 weeks, have you also been feeling depressed most of the day or lost interest in things you usually enjoy? If yes, has that been separate from the distress about your appearance, or mainly because of it?
I haven't really felt depressed in that way or lost interest in my hobbies. All of my distress and anxiety are completely focused on my appearance and how I look.

Besides worries about your appearance, do you also have other unwanted thoughts or rituals, like fears of contamination, needing things to be exact, or checking things over and over? Or are the repetitive thoughts and behaviors only about how you look?

No, I don't have any of those other worries like contamination or needing things to be exact. All of my rituals and repetitive thoughts are strictly focused on my appearance and trying to check or hide my flaws. I don't do those kinds of things for anything else.

Based on this conversation, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder seems unlikely because the intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors are exclusively centered on perceived appearance defects, with classic body-focused behaviors such as mirror checking, skin picking, comparing appearance, and reassurance seeking for several hours per day. The patient also reports that others see the nose as normal, supporting a preoccupation with perceived flaws. There are no broader OCD symptoms like contamination fears, symmetry concerns, or non-appearance-related compulsions. The candidate list is therefore narrowed to ["Body Dysmorphic Disorder"].
